name: correlation_strategies.json
description: Positive/negative correlation and divergence strategies with entry checklists and risk notes, plus sourced research context on why correlation is not cointegration.
summary: Correlation measures how consistently two assets' returns move together (-1 to +1). Positive-correlation strategies are for confirmation, concentrated exposure control and pairs trading; negative-correlation strategies are for hedging and diversification. Divergence strategies trade temporary breaks of the usual relationship.

scale.label: Strong positive
scale.example: Two large tech stocks, EUR/USD vs GBP/USD (historically about +0.8)

scale.label: Weak/moderate positive
scale.example: A stock and a broad index

scale.label: Strong negative
scale.example: Oil vs airline shares, USD index vs gold (often)

formulas.pearson: rho = Cov(Rx, Ry) / (sigma_x * sigma_y), computed on RETURNS not raw prices
formulas.spread: S_t = P_A,t - beta * P_B,t, with beta from regression (hedge ratio); or use log prices: ln(P_A) - beta*ln(P_B)
formulas.beta: beta = Cov(Ra, Rb) / Var(Rb)  or OLS slope of A on B
formulas.half_life: Fit dS_t = a + b*S_{t-1} + e; half_life = -ln(2)/b; use it to choose lookback and expected holding time

key_facts: Use returns or normalised prices; raw price correlation is spurious for trending series.
Use rolling windows (20, 30, 90 bars) and test several; correlation changes by regime.
Correlation is not causation and is not stable; crises raise correlations among risk assets.
A correlation of -0.7 does not mean opposite moves every day.

strategies.name: Trend confirmation
strategies.text: If related assets are positively correlated, a breakout in a leader supports a view in the follower. Example: semiconductor index breakout supports long in a major chip stock.
strategies.risk: A false signal in the leader transfers to the follower.

strategies.name: Momentum and sector rotation
strategies.text: Overweight the strongest positively correlated group (e.g. cyclicals in expansion) rather than spreading evenly.

strategies.name: Correlation-based position sizing
strategies.text: Three positions with correlation above about 0.7 are roughly one bet. Divide the risk budget among them. Portfolio variance = sum_i sum_j w_i w_j sigma_i sigma_j rho_ij.

strategies.name: Pairs trade (positive-correlation convergence)
setup: Pick two assets with strong, economically logical correlation (AUD/USD and NZD/USD; EUR/USD and GBP/USD; two same-sector stocks; two similar ETFs).
Spread stationary (Augmented Dickey-Fuller p < 0.05) or cointegrated (Engle-Granger or Johansen).
strategies.entry: Spread z-score beyond +/-1.5 to 2.0: short the outperformer and buy the underperformer, sized by hedge ratio beta.
strategies.exit: Spread returns to mean (z near 0) or partial reversion (z near 0.5). Time stop at about 2-3x half-life.
strategies.stop: z-score beyond 3 to 3.5 in the wrong direction, or correlation falls below a floor, or time stop.
strategies.example: AUD/USD rallies while NZD/USD barely moves; spread z = +2.3. Short AUD/USD, long NZD/USD.

strategies.name: Diversification with negatively/low-correlated assets
strategies.text: Combining imperfectly correlated assets lowers portfolio volatility. For two assets, minimum variance happens at weights that reduce the covariance term; negative rho gives the strongest reduction.
strategies.caution: Correlations rise in crises; stocks and bonds have not always been negatively correlated (e.g. inflationary periods).

strategies.name: Direct hedge
strategies.text: Hold an offsetting position (inverse instrument, option, negatively correlated asset) against existing exposure. Hedge ratio h = rho * (sigma_position / sigma_hedge) as a minimum-variance approximation.
strategies.trade_off: Reduces downside but lowers expected return and adds cost.

strategies.name: Currency and commodity hedges
strategies.text: Example: higher oil raises airline costs; an airline-exposed holder may hedge with a long oil position.

strategies.name: Defensive allocation
strategies.text: Shift part of allocation from highly correlated risky assets to cash, short-duration bonds, gold or defensive sectors when uncertainty rises. Safe-haven behaviour is not guaranteed.

divergence.definition: Divergence is not just 'prices differ'. It is when the expected directional relationship breaks down.

table.divergence_signal: One rises while the other falls, or one moves much more than the other

table.normal: One rises while the other falls
table.divergence_signal: Both rise, both fall, or the inverse link weakens sharply

positive_divergence_trade.logic: Convergence: buy laggard, short leader when spread is abnormal (about 2 standard deviations).
outcomes: Mean reversion (laggard catches up or leader reverses)
Regime change (relationship fails; spread keeps widening)

setups: Convergence: assets normally inverse move together; short the relatively stronger and buy the weaker expecting the inverse link to resume.
Breakout: if correlation breaks sharply (some methods use rolling correlation falling past about -0.5 or flipping sign), treat as regime shift and follow the strongest confirmed move.
negative_divergence_trade.example: Two assets normally at -0.80 both rally. Mean-reversion view: fade the stronger. Breakout view: trade the stronger trend and ask what new driver changed the link.

measurement: Rolling correlation over 30 or 90 bars; compute Z-score of current correlation versus its history; beyond +/-2 is unusual.
Normalised spread: use returns, z-scores or ratio; for different price levels never compare raw prices.
Entry beyond 1.5-2.0 standard deviations; exit at mean or 0.5 sd.
Stationarity test (ADF) and cointegration test before assuming mean reversion; a trending spread suggests a broken relationship.

smt_divergence.name: SMT divergence (smart money tool)
smt_divergence.text: Compare highly correlated instruments (e.g. two equity indices or EUR/USD vs GBP/USD). If one makes a new high and the other fails, treat as a warning of weakness, to be used with structure and levels, not alone.

strategy_table.action: Position for rising or falling cross-asset correlation (e.g. dispersion/correlation trades via options)

entry_checklist: Stable correlation over a relevant lookback.
Divergence statistically large (spread beyond about 2 sd).
Plausible reason for divergence (liquidity, news, positioning, earnings, macro, flow).
Defined invalidation level (z-stop, time stop, correlation floor).
Position sizing accounts for both legs losing.
risk_management: Correlation breakdown risk, spread expansion risk, timing risk, liquidity risk, event risk, hidden correlation risk.
Use volatility-based stops on the spread, not fixed currency stops.
Treat positions with correlation above about 0.7 as one exposure.
Avoid divergence trades right before major scheduled news unless it is the thesis.
Use divergence as confluence, not as a standalone signal.
Backtest across trending, choppy, high-volatility and crisis regimes.

python_snippets.rolling_correlation:
import pandas as pd
ret = prices.pct_change().dropna()
rho = ret['A'].rolling(30).corr(ret['B'])
python_snippets.hedge_ratio_and_spread:
import statsmodels.api as sm
X = sm.add_constant(prices['B'])
beta = sm.OLS(prices['A'], X).fit().params['B']
spread = prices['A'] - beta*prices['B']
z = (spread - spread.rolling(60).mean())/spread.rolling(60).std()
python_snippets.adf_test:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
p = adfuller(spread.dropna())[1]  # p < 0.05 suggests stationary
python_snippets.cointegration:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint
score, p, _ = coint(prices['A'], prices['B'])  # p < 0.05 suggests cointegration

deriv_note: Deriv synthetic indices are generated independently, so cross-index correlation is expected to be near zero by design; correlation/pairs strategies are meaningful on real markets (forex, stocks, indices, commodities) rather than between independent synthetics. Verify by measuring rho before assuming any link.

research_context: Correlation is not cointegration: only a stationary linear combination supports spread mean reversion, and cointegration relationships can break down, with out-of-sample deterioration documented in a PEP-KO case study.
Walk-forward evidence across seven US-listed pairs found a cointegration gate useful but not sufficient for profitability.
How pairs are pre-selected materially changes final profitability in cointegration-based studies.
application_to_this_app: NEEZY's pair_research estimates the hedge ratio on the training slice only and uses lagged z-scores; its six captured Forex experiments were net negative after assumed costs.
